title: On the Secrecy of the Encapsulation Coin in ML-KEM
authors: Madjid G. Tehrani, William J Buchanan, and Mouad Lemoudden
abstract: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) draws a fresh 32-byte coin at each encapsulation. The shared secret is a deterministic function of the public key and this coin, so a known coin is a recovered key. This is elementary. We ask instead how well the coin's secrecy is protected in practice, and we answer by experiment. On six unmodified libraries (OpenSSL 3.5, wolfSSL 5.9, AWS-LC, Go 1.26, Bouncy Castle 1.83, and CIRCL), and a from-scratch reference, the coin-recovery is reachable in every one; what differs is the guard, from a test-walled package in Go to an ordinary production call in wolfSSL. A second path needs no injection function at all: substituting the generator at build time makes the ordinary encapsulation predictable, while the public re-seed interface correctly refuses to. Outside the validated FIPS-140-3 configuration that most deployments do not yet use, the coin's secrecy rests on convention, not construction. The predictability this permits is externally invisible and parameter-controlled, of the class shown once before in Dual_EC_DRBG. We claim no backdoor; we claim only that the door is reachable, and say so while it is still being closed.

On the Secrecy of the Encapsulation Coin in ML-KEM
                      M. G. Tehrani∗             W. J. Buchanan†             M. Lemoudden‡



                                                      Abstract
          ML-KEM (FIPS 203) draws a fresh 32-byte coin at each encapsulation. The shared secret is a
          deterministic function of the public key and this coin, so a known coin is a recovered key. This is
          elementary. We ask instead how well the coin’s secrecy is protected in practice, and we answer by
          experiment. On six unmodified libraries (OpenSSL 3.5, wolfSSL 5.9, AWS-LC, Go 1.26, Bouncy
          Castle 1.83, and CIRCL), and a from-scratch reference, the coin-recovery is reachable in every
          one; what differs is the guard, from a test-walled package in Go to an ordinary production call
          in wolfSSL. A second path needs no injection function at all: substituting the generator at build
          time makes the ordinary encapsulation predictable, while the public re-seed interface correctly
          refuses to. Outside the validated FIPS-140-3 configuration that most deployments do not yet
          use, the coin’s secrecy rests on convention, not construction. The predictability this permits is
          externally invisible and parameter-controlled, of the class shown once before in Dual_EC_DRBG.
          We claim no backdoor; we claim only that the door is reachable, and say so while it is still being
          closed.


1        Introduction
The security of ML-KEM rests on a small amount of secret randomness: a 32-byte encapsulation
coin m drawn at each encapsulation, and two 32-byte coins d, z drawn at key generation. That the
scheme collapses if such a coin is known is not in dispute and not, by itself, interesting; it is an
immediate consequence of the standard’s algorithms being deterministic once the coin is fixed. The
standard accordingly instructs implementers to draw these coins from an approved cryptographic
generator. Yet every conforming implementation must also provide a way to supply a fixed coin,
because the Known-Answer Tests required for validation are defined in exactly those terms. The
coin is thus both the object that must remain secret and an input the implementation is obliged to
be able to set.
    This tension motivates our question:

          Is the randomness of ML-KEM a parameterisable point of failure? That is, do paths
          exist (whether through direct coin-injection functions, or through control of the generator
          itself ) by which the behaviour of encapsulation can be made fully predictable, without that
          manipulation being detectable from outside?

        We answer in the affirmative, and make the answer precise. Our contributions:

        • A leakage theorem (§2). We state, with a proof from the FIPS 203 internal algorithms,
          what the leakage of each coin yields: m breaks the corresponding session, d exposes accepted

      decapsulations, and z exposes the rejection branch, with full offline decapsulation requiring d
      and z together. We note in particular that the shared secret K is fixed by (ek, m) before the
      ciphertext exists, so recovery from m needs the public key and the coin, never the ciphertext.

    • A six-library reachability survey (§3, Table 1). We run the m-recovery attack end-
      to-end on six unmodified libraries and a reference implementation. All expose a reachable
      injection path; the libraries differ markedly in how that path is guarded, ranging from a
      test-only package (Go) through an exported “experimental” API (AWS-LC) to an ordinary
      production call (wolfSSL). The protection of the coin is, in these general-purpose builds, a
      matter of convention rather than construction.

    • The generator path, and its safe counterpart (§3). We show that predictability is
      also reachable with no injection function at all, by substituting the generator the ordinary
      encapsulation call draws from at build time; and we show that the matching public re-seed
      interface correctly refuses to do this. The danger therefore lies not in normal use but in control
      of the build or distribution chain. This is the same kind of externally invisible, parameter-
      controlled predictability seen historically in Dual_EC_DRBG [2, 3].

    • Where the doors come from (§4). We document, from NIST’s own standardisation
      record [8], that these deterministic entry points were added so that ML-KEM could be tested
      for validation. The risk we raise is not that they exist, but that the line between “present for
      testing” and “reachable in shipped code” is kept only by convention in the general-purpose
      builds most systems use today.

    We are deliberate about what we do not claim. We do not assert that any standard generator,
or ML-KEM itself, contains a deliberate backdoor; we have no such evidence and make no such
claim. We claim only that a mechanism for externally invisible, parameter-controlled predictability
exists and is reachable in deployed code, and that its existence deserves to be stated plainly while
validation of FIPS 203 modules (under which the direct hooks become unavailable) is still in progress
across the industry.
    We follow FIPS 203 [10]. Write B = {0, 1}8 for one byte and Bℓ for ℓ bytes. The scheme
fixes three hash maps built from Keccak: H = SHA3-256, G = SHA3-512, the implicit-rejection
map J = SHAKE256, and the extendable output function used for the matrix and noise. An
encapsulation key (public) is denoted ek; a decapsulation key (private) is dk. We use the FIPS 203
names Encaps, Decaps, KeyGen and their internal forms throughout, and refer to the standard’s own
algorithm numbers (e.g. Encaps_internal is Algorithm 17 of FIPS 203 [10]) rather than reprinting
them.
    Three 32-byte values are sampled uniformly at random in the scheme:
               $             $                                      $
            d ← B32 ,      z ← B32      (both in KeyGen),       m ← B32        (in Encaps).

Everything else (ek, dk, the ciphertext c, the shared secret K) is a deterministic function of these
three coins and the public parameters. This is the whole of what follows.


2    A leakage theorem
We fix the target. An adversary breaks ML-KEM if, given ek and a ciphertext c, it outputs the
shared secret that Decaps(dk, c) returns. The following theorem records what each of the three
coins yields. It is elementary, a direct reading of the deterministic FIPS 203 internal maps, and we

                                                   2
claim no novelty for it; we state it carefully because the empirical sections rest on its first part, and
because the three coins are not interchangeable.
Theorem 1 (Leakage of the internal randomness). Fix a well-formed encapsulation key ek, with
matching decapsulation key dk generated from seeds (d, z).
  (i) If the encapsulation coin m of Encaps(ek; m) is known to A, then A recomputes the ciphertext
      c and shared secret K with no interaction. For the matching dk, decapsulation of c returns
      this same K, except with the ML-KEM decapsulation-failure probability δ.
 (ii) If the key seed d is known to A, then A recomputes the K-PKE decryption key and hence the
      decapsulation output for every ciphertext that the re-encryption check accepts. For ciphertexts
      on the rejection branch, knowledge of z is required in addition.
(iii) If the rejection seed z is known to A, then A computes the decapsulation output J(z | c) for
      every ciphertext on the rejection branch. Knowledge of z alone does not determine the output
      on accepted ciphertexts.
Proof. (i). Encapsulation (FIPS 203 Algorithm 17 [10]) computes
                                        
                   (K, r) = G m | H(ek) ,     c = K-PKE.Encrypt(ek, m, r),
where G = SHA3-512 and H = SHA3-256 are the two Keccak hashes of FIPS 203, K-PKE.Encrypt
is the underlying public-key encryption (Algorithm 14), and | denotes byte-string concatenation.
Both are functions of (ek, m) alone, so A evaluates them and obtains (c, K) outright; the recov-
ery of K by A is exact. The honest receiver runs decapsulation (Algorithm 18): it computes
m′ = K-PKE.Decrypt(dkPKE , c), re-derives (K ′ , r′ ) = G(m′ | H(ek)), and returns K ′ when the re-
encryption matches c. Whenever m′ = m one has K ′ = K. The two parties therefore agree except
on the measure-δ set of decapsulation failures, where δ ≤ 2−138 for the three parameter sets [10];
the adversary’s own knowledge of K carries no such caveat.
    (ii). K-PKE.KeyGen (Algorithm 13) expands d deterministically into the secret vector and the
private key dkPKE = ByteEncode12 (ŝ). Holding d, A recomputes dkPKE , runs K-PKE.Decrypt on
any c to recover m′ , re-derives (K ′ , r′ ), and re-encrypts. On the accept branch this returns the
decapsulated key. The reject branch returns J(z | c), which d does not determine; hence d alone
covers exactly the accepted ciphertexts.
    (iii). On the reject branch, decapsulation returns K̄ = J(z | c), with J = SHAKE256, a function
of (z, c). Knowing z, A computes K̄ for any c that takes that branch. An honestly generated c passes
re-encryption and never reaches the branch, so z alone says nothing about accepted ciphertexts.

Remark 1. The three leakages are not equivalent. The coin m is per-encapsulation: its disclosure
breaks one session. The seed d is long-term key material: its disclosure exposes every accepted
decapsulation under ek. The seed z is long-term rejection material: its disclosure exposes only the
rejection branch. Full offline decapsulation of arbitrary ciphertexts requires enough to compute
both branches, that is, d together with z (equivalently, the stored seed pair, which FIPS 203 says
must be guarded as a decapsulation key [10]). The empirical part of this paper concerns case (i):
the per-session coin m, which is the one every surveyed library exposes.
Remark 2. K is the first half of G(m | H(ek)) and is fixed before c exists. In particular K is
a function of (m, ek) and is independent of the ciphertext c. A derivation of the form K =
SHAKE256(m | c) does not occur in FIPS 203 and is impossible by the ordering of FIPS 203 Algo-
rithm 17; we note it because the error is easy to make and changes nothing in case (i) except the
formula one computes.

                                                   3
Remark 3. Case (i) is the zero-query, chosen-coin setting. It is adjacent to, but distinct from,
the reuse attacks of Okada and Wang [11], which recover Bob’s randomness in Kyber and SABER
from a handful of decryption queries under a meta-PKE model. There the coin is secret but reused;
here it is simply known. The two results bound the same quantity, the cost of any failure of the
encapsulation coin, from opposite ends.


3    A concrete realisation of Theorem 1
FIPS 203, §6.2, sanctions one way to supply the encapsulation coin externally: the test param-
eter OSSL_KEM_PARAM_IKME (“m”), exposed by OpenSSL since version 3.5 [14]. Setting it makes
EVP_PKEY_encapsulate consume a caller-supplied m rather than drawing one from the library gen-
erator. We stress the negative companion fact: the default path obtains m from RAND_bytes_ex on
the library context’s DRBG, which no openssl.cnf setting redirects; configuration alone cannot
make encapsulation deterministic. The coin can leak only through the program interface or through
observation of the running process, which is exactly the threat Theorem 1 formalises.

Procedure. We generate an honest ML-KEM-768 key pair, fix a 32-byte file m, and encapsulate
twice against the public key with m supplied through the IKME parameter; then we decapsulate
the first ciphertext with the private key. The adversary’s view is (ek, m); the honest party’s view is
(dk, c).
# fixed coin m, deterministic encapsulation, honest decapsulation
./encap_ikme pk.pem m.bin ct1.bin ss_enc1.bin      # adversary path (run 1)
./encap_ikme pk.pem m.bin ct2.bin ss_enc2.bin      # adversary path (run 2)
openssl pkeyutl -decap -inkey sk.pem -in ct1.bin -secret ss_dec.bin

    We carried out the same procedure in a second, independent library, wolfSSL 5.9.1 [15], whose
with-randomness entry point wc_MlKemKey_EncapsulateWithRandom accepts the coin directly. Un-
like OpenSSL’s IKME, this is a documented production function, exposed for external-entropy (e.g.
quantum) integration rather than gated as test-only; the injection surface is therefore wider.

Observed. In both libraries the two encapsulations agreed, and the secret computed from (ek, m)
equalled the secret recovered from (dk, c). The wolfSSL run, with the fixed coin m = 4b4e...2121,
produced

        K = 8217d697668fa9fdd6145bb43866b335d550730a78ffd8a64e1cf36a1ab9d201,

identical on the encapsulation and decapsulation sides:

       check              OpenSSL 3.5 (IKME)       wolfSSL 5.9.1 (EncapsulateWithRandom)
       c1 = c2            yes                      yes
       Kenc,1 = Kenc,2    yes                      yes
       Kenc = Kdec        yes                      yes

The first two equalities show the coin was consumed; the third is Theorem 1 in a single line.
Consistently with Remark 2, K is fixed by (ek, m): re-deriving it requires the public key and the coin,
not the ciphertext. We ran the same experiment in four further implementations: AWS-LC[1] (via its
exported EVP_PKEY_encapsulate_deterministic), Go 1.26 (via the test-only mlkemtest package),
Bouncy Castle 1.83 [13] (via internalGenerateEncapsulated), and Cloudflare’s CIRCL [4] (via

the public EncapsulateTo and EncapsulateDeterministically); all produced Kenc = Kdec (§5).
Together with a from-scratch FIPS 203 reference in Python, seven independent implementations
agree on the same lemma, which indicates the effect is a property of the standard, not of any one
codebase.

The injection surface varies by library. The mechanism by which the coin can be supplied
externally, and whether that mechanism survives FIPS 140-3 validation, differs across implementa-
tions. Table 1 summarises the current state.

OpenSSL 3.5          OSSL_KEM_PARAM_IKME                  direct, test-only             module in process
wolfSSL 5.9          EncapsulateWithRandom                direct, production            in development
AWS-LC               EVP_PKEY_encapsulate_deterministic   direct, exported-experimental in CMVP process
Go 1.26              mlkemtest package only               direct, test-walled           module in process
Bouncy Castle 1.83   internalGenerateEncapsulated         direct, “internal” method     not validated
CIRCL (Cloudflare) EncapsulateTo, Encapsulate             direct, public production API not validated
                   Deterministically

Table 1: Reachability of the encapsulation coin across ML-KEM libraries, and how each claim here
is supported. The mechanism class ranges over: a parameter documented test-only (OpenSSL); a
plain production function (wolfSSL); an exported function placed in an experimental/ header and
named _deterministic (AWS-LC); a function reachable only from a separate package explicitly
labelled test-only (Go); and a method named internal taking the coin bytes directly (Bouncy
Castle); and a public production method on the standard interface (CIRCL). All six rows were
executed end-to-end on one machine (fixed m twice, then decapsulation with the private key, all
giving Kenc = Kdec ). wolfSSL and CIRCL expose the coin through ordinary production calls; the
others guard, label, or wall it off, yet in each the coin is reachable. In every validated FIPS-140-3
configuration the direct hooks are unavailable, since supplying caller-chosen bytes as the approved
RNG output is not an approved service; the variation above is in the general-purpose builds, which
is what most deployments use while validation of FIPS 203 modules is still in progress.


Scope. The constructions use no modified library code and no disabled safeguard; each uses a
documented entry point in the role it was built for. They say nothing about ML-KEM run with
a sound, secret coin, and nothing about the validated FIPS-140-3 configuration, where the direct
hooks are unavailable. They say only what Theorem 1 says: a known coin is a recovered key. The
point of Table 1 is orthogonal and sharper: the coin’s secrecy is, in several deployed libraries, a
matter of convention rather than of construction.

The generator path: predictability without any injection function. The table concerns
direct coin injection. A second, independent path is to leave the ordinary encapsulation call un-
touched and instead control the generator it draws from. We tested this in wolfSSL, whose normal
wc_MlKemKey_Encapsulate draws the coin via wc_RNG_GenerateBlock from a supplied WC_RNG. Two
sub-cases separate cleanly and instructively:

   • Public re-seed (safe). Re-seeding the DRBG through the public wc_RNG_DRBG_Reseed with
     a fixed value does not make the output predictable: two runs under the same fixed seed


                                                    5
      produced different shared secrets. The interface mixes the caller’s bytes with system entropy
      rather than replacing it, which is the correct DRBG behaviour.

    • Build-time generator substitution (predictable). wolfSSL’s documented CUSTOM_RAND_GENERATE_
      BLOCK build hook replaces the generator source outright. Compiling the library’s random.c
      with this macro pointed at a deterministic counter, the ordinary Encapsulate (no injection
      function) became fully reproducible: a party knowing only the generator parameter recom-
      puted the victim’s exact shared secret, while the key is indistinguishable from a sound one
      externally.

The contrast is the finding. Predictability here is not reachable through normal use of the public
API, but it is reachable by whoever controls the library build or distribution, the supply-chain
position. This is the same class of externally invisible, parameter-controlled predictability exhibited
historically by Dual_EC_DRBG; we claim the existence of the mechanism and its reachability, not
that any standard DRBG is itself compromised.


4    Why the functions exist, and the risk that they persist
It is worth being precise about where the deterministic entry points of Table 1 come from, because
the history is documented and the analogy we draw is a careful one.

They were created for standardisation testing. The injection functions are not accidental. In
the public comment period for FIPS 203, reviewers observed that the core ML-KEM algorithms are
hard to test precisely because they are non-deterministic. NIST’s response, recorded in the Federal
Register notice issuing the standard [8], was to split each function in two: “a deterministic function
that accepts randomness as input (to enable testing) and an externally callable function that gener-
ates the needed randomness.” This is exactly the shape we found in every library: Encaps_internal
(Algorithm 17 of FIPS 203 [10]) takes the coin as an argument so that the Known-Answer Tests
of the validation programs can supply a fixed value and check a fixed output. The doors exist by
design, and for a legitimate reason.

The standards bodies know they must not leak into production. The testing programs
are themselves aware that these internals are not for callers. In a 2025 NIST KEM workshop, the
validation community noted plans to add a test of the internal K-PKE encryption routine while
being “fully aware this algorithm is not allowed to be used directly by callers” [7]. The intended
boundary is explicit: the deterministic interface is a test artifact, the randomised interface is the
product.

The risk is that the boundary is forgotten. Our concern is not that the functions exist, but
that the line between “present for validation” and “reachable in shipped code” is maintained only by
convention in the general-purpose builds most deployments currently use. Table 1 shows the line
being drawn in four different places, and in one library (wolfSSL) not drawn at all. The cautionary
precedent is Dual_EC_DRBG, which entered the SP 800-90 standard through the normal process and
remained a recommended generator for roughly seven years before being withdrawn [2, 12]. Notably,
the researchers who first demonstrated its weakness did not claim an intentional backdoor; they
showed only that the design permitted one for whoever knew a secret parameter relation [12]. Our
claim about ML-KEM is of the same restrained form: a documented, legitimate testing mechanism
creates a parameter-controlled, externally invisible path to predictable keys, and the only thing

                                                  6
standing between that path and production deployment is developer discipline plus eventual FIPS-
140-3 validation, neither of which is yet universal. The door was opened for a good reason; the
danger is that it is left open after the reason has passed.


5    Reproducibility
All code, build scripts, and step-by-step guides are in a public repository:

                            https://github.com/owlmt/mlkempaper/

    The repository has one folder per experiment (the six libraries, the Python reference, and the
generator experiment), each with its own guide and the exact commands used. Every experiment
was run on Ubuntu 24.04 with the library versions named in Table 1. A run is successful when the
program prints YES on all three comparison lines: the two encapsulations under a fixed coin agree,
and decapsulation with the private key recovers the same shared secret.
    We note our process openly: the code, the per-experiment documentation, the repository’s
commit and push steps, and the cross-checking of each experiment’s output were carried out with
the assistance of an AI coding assistant, and then verified by hand against the library sources and
the FIPS 203 algorithm definitions.

Future directions. Two extensions follow naturally. First, the construction this paper con-
cerns is not unique to one protocol: the concatenation of an ML-KEM shared secret with a tradi-
tional secret recurs in TLS 1.3, in SSH (draft-ietf-sshm-mlkem-hybrid-kex)[6], and in IKEv2
(draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem)[5], each of which derives session keys from a shared secret
that a known coin would make predictable at the layer beneath. We examine the protocol-level
consequences, and the differing exposure of pure versus hybrid key establishment, separately. Sec-
ond, the reachability question we ask of ML-KEM applies equally to ML-DSA (FIPS 204)[9], whose
signing procedure likewise admits a deterministic, externally supplied randomness input introduced
for known-answer testing; whether deployed libraries guard that input by convention or by con-
struction, and what a controlled value there permits, is a parallel evaluation we intend to carry
out.


6    Conclusion
The shared secret of ML-KEM is fixed by the public key and a single 32-byte coin, so a known
coin is a recovered key; this is elementary, and not our point. Our point is empirical: across
six independent, unmodified libraries and a reference implementation, a path to fix that coin is
reachable in every one, and the only barrier between that path and a predictable production key is
convention, developer discipline, and a FIPS-140-3 validation that most current deployments have
not yet completed. We make no claim of a backdoor in ML-KEM or in any generator; we claim only
that the mechanism for externally invisible, parameter-controlled predictability exists, is reachable
today, and is of the same class history has already shown us once in Dual_EC_DRBG, and that it
deserves to be named while the doors are still being closed.
